title: From Zero to Your First Paid AI Project
description: A personal plan that takes you from «I know some AI tools» to money in your account. Built from your answers: what you want to sell, how much time you have, and what is stopping you right now.

modules.title: How AI Freelancing Actually Works
modules.description: See how AI work is really bought and sold — without the hype or the six-figure screenshots. Covers what clients pay for, what they ignore, and the shortest honest path to a first paid task.

lessons.title: Why Your AI Skills Aren't Getting You Paid

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Most people approach this in the same order: learn the tools first, then look for work. It sounds sensible. You would not apply for a driving job without knowing how to drive.

But the people getting paid right now are rarely the ones who know the most tools. They are the ones who can name a job a business already wants done, and say they will do it. The skill is the easy half. The hard half is the sentence you send.

blocks.heading: Clients Don't Buy Tools
blocks.bodyHtml:
A business owner does not wake up wanting AI. They wake up with a newsletter that has not gone out for three weeks.

Compare two replies to the same job post:

«I'm an AI specialist skilled in ChatGPT, Claude and Midjourney.»

«I'll write your weekly newsletter in your voice and hand it over ready to send.»

The first one asks the buyer to imagine what you might do. The second one describes their Tuesday without the problem in it.

blocks.text: Nobody pays for access to a tool they could open themselves.

blocks.heading: The Gap Nobody Warns You About
blocks.bodyHtml:
Here is where most beginners actually stall, and none of it is about skill:

  • No named service — «I can do anything with AI» reads as «I have done nothing yet»
  • No proof — nothing a stranger can look at in ten seconds
  • No price — every conversation stops at «it depends»
  • No routine — five applications in a burst, then nothing for two weeks

Each of these is a sentence you have not written yet. That is genuinely all. Nothing here requires another course.

blocks.question: A business owner posts: «Need help with our weekly newsletter.» Which first reply is strongest?

options.label: I'm an AI specialist with experience in ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini.
I'll write your weekly newsletter in your voice, ready to publish.
I use advanced prompt engineering to produce content very fast.
I've completed several courses on AI writing and content design.

blocks.successBody: The buyer has a job to hand over, not a tool to learn. Naming the finished thing — a newsletter in their voice, ready to send — is what makes a reply feel like relief instead of homework.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about what the person on the other side wants to stop doing themselves this week.

blocks.heading: What a Buyer Checks First
blocks.bodyHtml:
When someone reads your message, they are answering three questions in about eight seconds:

  • Did they understand my problem? Your first line should sound like their job post, not your CV.
  • Have they done this before? One relevant example beats a list of ten unrelated ones.
  • Will this be easy? A clear next step — a price, a timeline, one question — removes the work of deciding.

Notice that none of the three asks which model you used.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Open any freelance platform and read five job posts in a field that interests you.
Copy the exact words buyers use for the outcome they want — not the tools they name.
Write one sentence that offers that outcome, with no tool mentioned at all.
Read it out loud. If it sounds like a description of you rather than of their week, rewrite it.

blocks.heading: The Shortest Honest Path
blocks.bodyHtml:
You do not need to be the best AI operator available. You need to be the person who removes one specific job from someone's week, reliably, for a price they can approve without a meeting.

That is a much smaller target than it first appears. And it is reachable in weeks, not years, because the bar is not talent — it is clarity.

blocks.body: People are not buying AI skills; they are buying a task leaving their list. Skill gets you ready, but a named service, visible proof, a stated price and a weekly routine are what get you paid. Every one of those is a sentence you can write today.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: why charging for hours quietly caps what you can earn — and what to sell instead.

lessons.title: Why Charging for Hours Holds You Back

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Hourly rates feel like the fair way to start. You are new, you do not want to overcharge, and time is something both sides understand.

But there is a trap inside it. AI makes you faster every month — and an hourly rate turns that speed into a pay cut. Finish in one hour what used to take four, and you have just charged yourself a quarter of the fee for the same result.

blocks.heading: The Same Job, Two Ways
blocks.bodyHtml:
A client needs twelve product descriptions. Look at the difference in what you are actually selling:

«£20 per hour, roughly six hours.»

«£180 for twelve product descriptions, delivered Thursday, one round of revisions included.»

The first invites a negotiation about your speed. The second invites a decision about a result. Only one of them gets faster to answer as you get better.

blocks.text: Price the result, and speed becomes your profit instead of your penalty.

blocks.heading: What a Fixed Price Needs
blocks.bodyHtml:
A price is only safe when the shape of the job is decided. Three things do that:

  • A number. Twelve descriptions. Four posts. One landing page. Not «content support».
  • A date. Thursday. Not «soon» — vagueness costs you the weekend.
  • A limit. One round of revisions included, further rounds charged. This single line prevents most unpaid work.

Miss one and the job expands quietly until the fee stops making sense.

blocks.question: You've quoted a fixed price. The client asks for a fifth round of edits. What's the professional move?

options.label: Do them quietly — arguing over edits will only damage the relationship.
Point to the agreed limit and quote a small fee for the extra round.
Explain that AI-assisted work cannot really be revised that many times.
Switch this client to an hourly rate so the extra time gets covered.

blocks.successBody: The limit you agreed is what makes a fixed price work for both sides. Naming it calmly and offering the extra round as a small paid add-on keeps the job profitable without turning it into a conflict.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which answer protects both the relationship and the fee at the same time.

blocks.heading: Packaging Beats Guessing
blocks.bodyHtml:
Once you have priced the same job three times, stop quoting from scratch. Write it down as a package with a name, a scope and a number.

Two effects follow immediately. Buyers decide faster, because there is nothing to work out. And you stop under-pricing on tired days, because the number is no longer a judgement call you make in the moment.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Pick one job you could deliver this week and write it as: quantity, deadline, revision limit.
Put a number on it — the one you would accept without hesitating, not the lowest you would tolerate.
Read the package back and ask whether a stranger could approve it without a call.
If they could not, the scope is still too vague — add the missing number or date.

blocks.heading: When Hourly Still Makes Sense
blocks.bodyHtml:
There is one honest exception: work whose shape genuinely cannot be known in advance. Ongoing support, exploratory research, sitting inside someone else's messy process.

For that, bill by time — but cap it. «Up to eight hours a month, reviewed together before we go over» keeps the openness without handing the client an unlimited claim on your week.

blocks.body: Hourly billing punishes the speed AI gives you. Price the result instead, and make the result safe to price with three details: a quantity, a date and a revision limit. Keep time-based billing only for work whose shape genuinely cannot be known, and cap it.

lessons.title: Your First Paid Task in One Week

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
The advice you usually get is to build a portfolio, then a website, then a brand, and eventually approach clients. It sounds responsible. It is also why most people are still preparing a year later.

There is a shorter route, and it is not a shortcut in the bad sense. It works because a first paid task teaches you more in three days than three months of preparing for one.

blocks.heading: Start From the Task, Not the Career
blocks.bodyHtml:
A first job does not need to fit your long-term plan. It needs to be small, describable and finishable.

«I'm building an AI content agency.»

«I'll turn your ten blog posts into ten LinkedIn posts by Friday for £120.»

The second one can be accepted by a real person today. The first one cannot be accepted at all — there is nothing in it to say yes to.

blocks.text: A career is built out of finished jobs, not out of plans for them.

blocks.heading: The Week, Day by Day
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Days 1–2. Choose one task you can already do well. Write it as quantity, deadline, price.
  • Day 3. Make one sample of it — for a real company you admire, unpaid, unasked. This is your proof.
  • Days 4–6. Send fifteen messages: platform posts, past colleagues, local businesses. Same offer, same sample.
  • Day 7. Follow up with everyone who did not reply. Most first jobs come from the follow-up.

blocks.question: You've sent fifteen messages and received two polite refusals and no other replies. What does that mean?

options.label: The offer is wrong and should be rebuilt from scratch before sending more.
This is a normal week — follow up, then send the next fifteen messages.
The market is saturated and this kind of work is no longer worth selling.
You need a finished website and brand before anyone will take you seriously.

blocks.successBody: Fifteen messages is a small sample, not a verdict. Replies usually arrive after a follow-up, and the second batch tends to be better written than the first — which is exactly how the offer gets sharper.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about how many attempts it takes before you have enough information to judge anything.

blocks.heading: Why the Sample Does the Selling
blocks.bodyHtml:
An unrequested sample answers the only question that matters — can this person actually do the thing — before anyone has to trust you.

It also changes the tone of your message. You are no longer asking for a chance; you are showing something you already made and offering more of it. That difference is felt immediately by the person reading.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Name the task you could deliver this week, in one sentence a stranger would understand.
Pick one real company and make a small sample of that work for them today.
Write the message you'd attach it to — three sentences, no CV, one clear price.
Send it to five people before you allow yourself to edit it again.

blocks.heading: What Counts as Done
blocks.bodyHtml:
The goal of this week is not a good income. It is one transaction: someone paid you, you delivered, both sides were fine with it.

That single event changes what you can say next. You stop describing what you could do and start describing what you have done — and every message after it is easier to write.

blocks.body: The fastest route to a first paid task is a small, describable job, one unrequested sample and fifteen honest messages with a follow-up. Preparation feels safer, but a completed transaction teaches more and changes how you are able to describe yourself.
